claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element, nearly equiatomic automotive alloy catalyst without rare-earth dopants.
Adding 2–5 wt% La during synthesis and subsequently annealing the catalyst will selectively segregate La to grain boundaries.
La segregation will form finely dispersed, La-rich interfacial phases at grain boundaries.
The La-rich interfacial phases can remain thin enough not to block surface active sites.
La-rich interfacial phases inhibit catalyst sintering.
Inhibiting sintering preserves the dispersion of active catalytic sites.
High active-site dispersion supports efficient catalytic performance.
La-rich interfacial phases electronically modify the catalyst and enhance its redox properties.
Annealing at approximately 600 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere containing controlled H2O and NO will drive La primarily to grain boundaries without producing an active-site-blocking overgrowth.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, La doping will improve low-temperature catalytic activity.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, La doping will improve durability during accelerated aging and transient exhaust operation.
The La-doped catalyst will resist degradation caused by H2O, NO, and thermal aging.
The La-doped catalyst will lose less active surface area than the untreated catalyst.
Improved stabilization and activity will enable lower platinum-group-metal loadings.
An untreated multi-element catalyst is likely to sinter and undergo active-site agglomeration under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
Sintering and active-site agglomeration in the untreated catalyst will cause substantial activity loss and reduced durability.
The intervention is applicable specifically to catalysts with nearly equiatomic compositions when La is maintained between 2 and 5 wt%.
La contents above 5 wt% may form an excessively thick La-rich phase that impedes reactant access.
Prior literature on rare-earth dopants in similar systems supports the proposed mechanism.
